problem_motivation.content: Further optimization steps are needed for the base alloy despite its good mechanical properties at elevated temperatures.
problem_motivation.evidence_span: arose the need of accomplishing further optimization steps

problem_motivation.content: There is a gap in high-temperature materials between steels and nickel-based superalloys that could be filled by less cost-intensive alloys.
problem_motivation.evidence_span: In the domain of high-temperature materials a gap between steels (<650 °C) and nickel-based superalloys (>850 °C) might be filled by less cost-intensive compositionally complex alloys.

problem_motivation.content: There is a need to improve the mechanical properties of compositionally complex alloys, specifically in the high-temperature range around 700–800 °C.
problem_motivation.evidence_span: In this work, compositionally complex alloys were improved with the goal to increase mechanical properties in the temperature range around 700–800 °C.

prior_approach.content: Previous studies have shown positive effects on mechanical properties of Ni-based superalloys through the addition of hafnium and molybdenum.
prior_approach.evidence_span: because of their well-known positive effects on mechanical properties of Ni-based superalloys

prior_approach.content: Yeh and Cantor first examined multicomponent alloys, with Cantor identifying a five-component alloy that forms a single-phase solid solution.
prior_approach.evidence_span: Multicomponent alloys were examined first by Yeh [ [2] ] and Cantor [ [3] ]. Investigating the microstructure of alloys with different numbers of elements in equiatomic mixtures, Cantor found the five-component, equiatomic alloy Co 20 Cr 20 Fe 20 Mn 20 Ni 20 to form a single-phase solid-solution.

prior_approach.content: Singh et al. examined the solidification behavior of the AlCoCrCuFeNi alloy using various microstructure analysis techniques.
prior_approach.evidence_span: Singh et al. [ [9] ] examined the six-component, equiatomic alloy AlCoCrCuFeNi, with a focus on solidification behavior, using different techniques to analyze the microstructure.

prior_approach.content: Researchers have optimized AlCoCrCuFeNi-based alloys by varying composition and heat treatment to achieve L12-ordered precipitates.
prior_approach.evidence_span: Much effort was put into optimizing alloys with near equiatomic composition of AlCoCrCuFeNi, investigating changes in composition and finding correct heat treatment parameters [ [10] ], resulting in the chemical composition Al 10 Co 25 Cr 8 Fe 15 Ni 36 Ti 6 (in at.%).

prior_approach.content: It is established that avoiding 45-degree grain boundaries relative to the loading direction eliminates shear stresses and improves strength.
prior_approach.evidence_span: Avoiding grain boundaries inclined at 45° by the loading direction, shear stresses along these weaker boundaries can be eliminated and the strength is just defined by the microstructure inside of the longitudinal orientated grains [ [11] ].

prior_limitation.content: Most multi-element alloys in near equiatomic composition do not form single-phase solid solutions but instead form intermetallic compounds.
prior_limitation.evidence_span: Most alloys containing at least five elements in near equiatomic composition, however, do not crystallize as a single-phase solid-solution, but rather form intermetallic compounds as secondary phases with even lower Gibbs free energy.

prior_limitation.content: High cooling rates like splat-quenching fail to achieve the expected solid-solution stabilization and instead cause phase decomposition.
prior_limitation.evidence_span: Even a high cooling rate by splat-quenching leads to a phase decomposition and the cast alloy shows a microstructure with several phases of different crystal structures, unlike expected solid-solution stabilization due to a high configurational entropy.

prior_limitation.content: Round γ′-particles contribute negatively to mechanical behavior, as observed when the base alloy and Mo-containing alloy exhibited similar characteristics with round particles.
prior_limitation.evidence_span: Since the base and the Mo-containing alloy (950 °C/50 h) showed the same characteristics of the Heusler type phase, round γ′-particles contributed in a bad way to the mechanical behavior.

causal_claim.content: Directional solidification resulted in an increase of tensile strength by a factor of 1.7 at room temperature and 1.8 at 600 °C.
causal_claim.evidence_span: Casting by the Bridgman process lead to a directionally solidified microstructure and an increase of strength in the direction of the grains by a factor of 1.7 at RT and 1.8 at 600 °C.

causal_claim.content: Mo addition lowered the ultimate tensile strength of the base alloy due to the more round morphology of γ′-particles.
causal_claim.evidence_span: Under the same heat treatment conditions, Mo addition lowered the ultimate tensile strength of the base alloy due to the more round morphology of γ′-particles.

causal_claim.content: The Hf-containing alloy showed an increase in UTS due to the lower content and/or the spherical shape of Heusler type phase.
causal_claim.evidence_span: The Hf-containing alloy, however, showed an increase in UTS due to the lower content and/or the spherical shape of Heusler type phase.

mechanism_principle.content: Molybdenum is expected to strengthen the lattice via solid-solution strengthening due to its larger atomic size causing distortion.
mechanism_principle.evidence_span: Molybdenum is supposed to partition to the matrix, to have a solid-solution strengthening effect due to its bigger atomic size and therefore to lead to a distorted lattice, acting as an obstacle for dislocation movement [ [12] ].

mechanism_principle.content: Hafnium strengthens grain boundaries by participating in the gamma prime phase, creating an interlocking configuration that retards fracture.
mechanism_principle.evidence_span: Doherty et al. [ [14] ] explain this by Hf participating more likely to the γ′-phase Ni 3 (Al, Hf), leading to a strengthening of it. The grain boundaries are therefore strengthened by the fracture-retarding effect of the interlocking γ′-configuration in this areas [ [15] ].

mechanism_principle.content: The desirable mechanical behavior of the base alloy after annealing at 900 °C/50 h is attributed to a drastic reduction in the volume content of Heusler type phase.
mechanism_principle.evidence_span: The reason for this desirable behavior was due to the volume content of Heusler type phase that was drastically reduced from 9% to 3% after annealing at 900 °C/50 h, see Table 3 .

hypothesis_statement.content: Good high-temperature tensile properties are expected if cubic precipitates are present and the Heusler type phase content is kept low.
hypothesis_statement.evidence_span: Consequently, good high-temperature tensile properties occurred in the case of cubic precipitates, assumed that the Heusler type phase content was kept quite low.

evidence_result.content: The base alloy's ultimate tensile strength exceeded that of Alloy 800 H across the entire tested temperature range.
evidence_result.evidence_span: While the base alloy showed UTS exceeding that of Alloy 800 H over the whole temperature range, it was very similar or only a little worse than the UTS of the alloy Inconel 617 at temperatures up to 700 °C.

evidence_result.content: In the 700–800 °C range, the base alloy's yield strength exceeded that of Inconel 617 by a factor of about 1.7 at 700 °C and 1.5 at 800 °C.
evidence_result.evidence_span: In the important temperature range the yield strength of the base alloy overran IN 617 by a factor of about 1.7 at 700 °C and 1.5 at 800 °C.

constraint.evidence_span: After evacuating the chamber twice to a pressure of 5∙10 −4 mbar it was flooded with argon to prevent the evaporation of elements

constraint.content: The mold withdrawal speed is constrained to 3 mm/min to achieve directional solidification.
constraint.evidence_span: the mold was withdrawn through a water cooled baffle with a speed of 3 mm/min

constraint.content: Homogenization times and temperatures are constrained to specific values to avoid eutectic formation.
constraint.evidence_span: homogenized for 20 h at 1220 °C in the case of the Mo-containing alloy and at 1140 °C in the case of the Hf-containing alloy to avoid eutectic formation

contradiction.content: Contrary to the expectation that larger precipitates would improve strength, increasing annealing time and temperature for Mo- and Hf-containing alloys led to a decrease in volume fractions of γ′-phase and no enhancement in Heusler type phase, unlike the base alloy.
contradiction.evidence_span: While the size of precipitates increased with longer treatment at higher temperatures for the Mo- and Hf-containing alloys, too, the volume fractions of the Heusler type phase and γ′-phase were not enhanced, but decreased about 7–8% in the case of the γ′-phase and remained constant in the case of the Heusler type phase.

questions.question: Does the morphology transition from cubic to round γ′-particles in AlCoCrCuFeNi-based alloys under 900 °C/50 h annealing occur at a specific critical volume fraction of Heusler phase that defines a strength boundary, or is the rounding caused primarily by the presence of Mo/Hf?
questions.rationale: The paper reports that round γ′-particles reduce strength, but the mechanism (morphology vs. Heusler fraction) is conflated for Mo/Hf alloys, while the base alloy improved with Heusler reduction. Distinguishing the critical boundary between these effects is essential to optimize alloying without sacrificing precipitate shape.
questions.decision_use: If the boundary is morphology-driven regardless of Heusler content, further optimization must target precipitate shape control (e.g., via heat treatment kinetics) rather than just phase volume reduction.
answer_requirements: Quantitative measurement of γ′-particle aspect ratio vs. Heusler phase volume fraction across a gradient of annealing temperatures for Mo- and Hf-containing alloys, followed by tensile testing at 700 °C.
evidence_spans: Since the base and the Mo-containing alloy (950 °C/50 h) showed the same characteristics of the Heusler type phase, round γ′-particles contributed in a bad way to the mechanical behavior.
Consequently, good high-temperature tensile properties occurred in the case of cubic precipitates, assumed that the Heusler type phase content was kept quite low.

questions.question: In AlCoCrCuFeNi-based alloys, does the addition of Mo degrade tensile strength at 700–800 °C by suppressing γ′-phase volume fraction or by inducing a detrimental round morphology, and how does this compare to the Hf effect?
questions.rationale: The paper attributes strength loss in Mo-alloys to round morphology but notes that Heusler fraction remained constant, whereas Hf alloys improved with lower Heusler content. Clarifying the primary causal factor (morphology vs. volume fraction) determines whether Mo should be replaced or if processing must be altered to preserve cubic shapes.
questions.decision_use: If morphology is the primary culprit, heat treatment protocols must be redesigned for Mo-alloys to maintain cubic precipitates, whereas if volume fraction is key, composition or annealing time must be adjusted.
answer_requirements: Comparative analysis of γ′-volume fraction and aspect ratio vs. UTS for Mo- and Hf-containing alloys after identical heat treatments, isolating the variable of alloying element.
evidence_spans: Under the same heat treatment conditions, Mo addition lowered the ultimate tensile strength of the base alloy due to the more round morphology of γ′-particles.
The Hf-containing alloy, however, showed an increase in UTS due to the lower content and/or the spherical shape of Heusler type phase.

While the size of precipitates increased with longer treatment at higher temperatures for the Mo- and Hf-containing alloys, too, the volume fractions of the Heusler type phase and γ′-phase were not enhanced, but decreased about 7–8% in the case of the γ′-phase and remained constant in the case of the Heusler type phase.
